ending: Lily's search for her mother ends in hard truth and unexpected peace. She learns from August that her mother, Deborah, had once lived with the Boatwright sisters, and that in a time of despair Deborah had left Lily behind for a period before meaning to return for her, a revelation that first devastates Lily and then, gradually, frees her from her guilt and idealized longing. Along the way the household suffers its own loss when the tender, sorrow-stricken May drowns herself, unable to bear the weight of the world's pain. When T. Ray finally traces Lily to Tiburon and comes to take her home, a tense confrontation follows, but August and the community of women refuse to give her up, and T. Ray, shaken, leaves her behind. Lily stays with the Boatwright sisters, embraced by August and by the circle of women known as the Daughters of Mary. Surrounded at last by mothers of every kind, she settles into a true home, having forgiven her mother, herself, and even, in part, the father who could not love her.
in_short: In 1964 South Carolina, fourteen-year-old Lily Owens lives with her cruel father and is tormented by the belief that she caused her mother's death as a small child. After her Black caretaker, Rosaleen, is beaten and jailed for defying local racists, Lily helps her escape, and the two run away, following a clue from her mother's belongings: a picture of a Black Madonna labeled with the town of Tiburon. There they are taken in by three Black beekeeping sisters, August, June, and May Boatwright, whose home centers on honey and a beloved Black Madonna statue. Lily learns beekeeping, finds friendship with a boy named Zach, and slowly heals among the women and their circle. Grief overtakes the fragile May, who takes her own life. Lily discovers that August had known her mother, who once stayed with the sisters, and confronts painful truths about her. When her father tracks her down, the sisters stand with Lily, and she is allowed to remain, finding at last the mothering and belonging she has always craved.

recaps.text: It is the summer of 1964 in Sylvan, South Carolina, and fourteen-year-old Lily Owens lives on a peach farm with her harsh, unloving father and the family's Black housekeeper, Rosaleen, who has helped raise her. Lily is tormented by a memory of the day her mother died, believing she was somehow the cause, and she treasures a small box of her mother's things, including a picture of a dark-skinned Madonna with the words 'Tiburon, S.C.' written on the back. When the newly passed civil rights law emboldens Rosaleen to go and register to vote, she is set upon and arrested after standing up to a group of white men, then beaten. Fearing for Rosaleen's life and desperate to escape her father, Lily sneaks her out and the two flee together, heading for Tiburon, the one clue Lily has to her mother's past.

In Tiburon, Lily follows the Black Madonna image on a jar of honey to the bright pink house of the Boatwright sisters, three Black women who keep bees and sell honey. The eldest, August, calm and perceptive, takes Lily and Rosaleen in, seemingly seeing through Lily's invented story about being an orphan on her way to an aunt. Lily begins learning the patient work of beekeeping at August's side and settles into the rhythms of the household, which include the proud, standoffish June and the tenderhearted, easily overwhelmed May. The home's spiritual heart is a battered wooden statue of a Black Madonna the women revere. Among the bees and the women's rituals, Lily starts to feel, for the first time, something like belonging, even as she hides the truth of who she is and why the town's name meant so much to her mother.

Lily grows into the life of the pink house, working the hives, absorbing August's quiet lessons about bees and about people, and joining the circle of churchwomen known as the Daughters of Mary who gather around the Black Madonna. She befriends Zach, the serious young man who helps August with the bees and dreams of becoming a lawyer, and the two grow close despite the dangers such a friendship carries in the segregated South. Lily begins to sense that August knows more about her than she lets on and that her mother's connection to this house runs deep. Torn between the fear of being discovered and a longing to ask outright, Lily keeps her secret a little longer, even as small signs point her toward the answers she both wants and dreads about her mother's past.

The fragile peace of the household is broken by cruelty and loss. Racial tensions in the town flare, and Zach is jailed after an incident, badly frightening everyone. The news, on top of a lifetime of accumulated sorrow, proves too much for the delicate May, who has always felt others' pain as her own; she walks down to the river and drowns herself, leaving a note asking to be let go and urging the others to be happy. The family is plunged into mourning, and the women hold a vigil over her. In the aftermath, the bonds among them tighten, June softens, and Lily, sharing in their grief, draws still closer to the truth of her own mother's history, feeling the moment approaching when she will finally have to reveal who she really is.

Lily at last confesses to August who she is, and August reveals that she had recognized her all along: she had once been a servant to Lily's mother's family and had known Deborah well, for Deborah had lived with the Boatwright sisters during a low point in her life. Lily learns the painful truth that her mother, overwhelmed and unwell, had once left her behind before intending to come back for her, and the knowledge first shatters and then slowly heals Lily, easing the guilt she has carried. When T. Ray finally tracks Lily to the pink house and comes to drag her home, the sisters and the Daughters of Mary stand firmly with her, and a shaken T. Ray leaves without her. Lily remains with the Boatwrights, surrounded by a community of women who become her mothers, having forgiven her mother and herself and found, at last, a real home and a place to belong.
